Binaries are attached to the release rather than committed, because cross-compiling a signed installer for another OS is not something a repository should fake. --- ## Roadmap See [ENHANCEMENTS.md](ENHANCEMENTS.md) for the full, costed list. The short version: - Share links with compressed project state in the URL · harmonic/percussive separation - ~~Optional sample pack~~ — shipped in 1.3.0: `pack/neonboom-pack-v1.zip`, auto-used by bundled builds --- ## License **PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0** — free for personal, hobby, study, teaching, research and non-profit/government use. Commercial use needs a separate licence; [open an issue](https://github.com/drsamonline/neonboom/issues) or email. ``` Required Notice: Copyright Dr Sohil Momin (https://github.com/drsamonline) ``` Full text: [LICENSE](LICENSE) · [polyformproject.org](https://polyformproject.org/licenses/noncommercial/1.0.0) ## Attribution No third-party code, fonts, sample packs or impulse responses are bundled. Every sound is generated at runtime by `src/audio/synth.js`; the reverb impulse is synthesised noise. The techniques follow public documentation (W3C Web Audio spec, MDN) and the books listed in [CREDITS.md](CREDITS.md) — including *The Audio Programming Book* (Boulanger & Lazzarini, MIT Press), *Web Audio API* (Boris Smus, O'Reilly), *Designing Sound* (Andy Farnell, MIT Press) and *Musimathics* (Gareth Loy, MIT Press). ## Sponsor NEONBOOM has no ads, no accounts and no analytics, which also means no revenue. If it is useful to you: - ⭐ star the repo and send it to someone who makes beats - 🐛 [report a bug](https://github.com/drsamonline/neonboom/issues) with the browser and what you expected - ♥ [sponsor the work](https://github.com/sponsors/drsamonline) — it buys the time to keep it dependency-free ## Author **Dr Sohil Momin** [sohilmomin2000@gmail.com](mailto:sohilmomin2000@gmail.com) · [github.com/drsamonline](https://github.com/drsamonline)
Built with the Web Audio API, a canvas and no dependencies. No cookies, no tracking, no upload.
offline-pdf-toolkit: # Offline PDF Toolkit [![License: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-blue)](LICENSE) **Merge, split, rotate, watermark, number, protect and compress PDFs — in one small page, with no server to send them to.** The page itself is about **49 KB gzipped**; the PDF engines load only when you open a document, and the OCR and qpdf engines only when you ask for them. No upload, no account, no tracking, no install. Unplug the network and it still works. **[Open the toolkit →](https://drsamonline.github.io/offline-pdf-toolkit/play/)** · [landing page](https://drsamonline.github.io/offline-pdf-toolkit/) · [downloads](#downloads) · [what's planned](ENHANCEMENTS.md) ![Screenshot](docs/shot.png) ## Why it exists The files people merge and split are usually the ones they should not hand to a stranger's server — patient reports, contracts, statements, identity documents. Every "free PDF tool" online uploads your file. This one cannot: the PDF engine is compiled into a single HTML file and there is no backend to send anything to. The proof is that it runs with the cable pulled out. | | | | |---|---|---| | ![The launcher, with no document open](docs/assets/app-home-desktop.png) | ![The launcher on a phone](docs/assets/app-home-mobile.png) | ![The app with five sample pages loaded](docs/assets/app-desktop.png) | The empty state is the front door: drop a file on the hero, or take one of the four tools a report usually needs. Every tool in the app is in one catalogue — the launcher, the all-tools sheet and the category dot beside each sidebar section all read from it. ## Features | | | |---|---| | **Launcher** | The empty state offers a drop target, the last files this tab wrote, and four core tools in one tap. Choose a tool with nothing open and it asks for the file, then opens itself. | | **All tools** | 27 tools in one sheet, grouped Edit / Optimize / Secure / Convert / Trust, with search. | | **Session list** | Every file the app writes, with the tool that made it and its size — in `sessionStorage`, so it dies with the tab, and the bytes are never kept. | | **Merge** | Add several PDFs; they lay out in order. Drag any page to reorder. | | **Split / extract** | Select pages (shift-click for a range) and pull them into a new PDF. | | **Rotate** | 90° steps, left or right, per page or for a whole selection. | | **Reorder / duplicate / delete** | Drag and drop, or move selections earlier/later. | | **Trim & resize** | Cut the same margin off every edge, or re-lay mixed pages onto A4 / Letter — text stays selectable. | | **Impose** | 2-up, 4-up and saddle-stitch booklet on A4 landscape sheets. | | **Watermark** | Text, centre / tiled / corner, with size, opacity, angle and colour. | | **Header & footer** | Six positions, with `{n}`, `{total}`, `{date}` and `{file}` tokens. | | **Bates numbering** | Prefix, start, zero-padded digits, four positions. | | **Split** | Every N pages, one file per page, or ranges (`1-3, 4, 8-10`). | | **Export images** | Every page as a PNG at the DPI you choose. | | **Redaction** | Cover every match of a word — or of a shape: 12-digit numbers, phone numbers, emails, PAN, dates, IFSC, and labelled identifiers (MRN, UHID, OPD, policy). With *rebuild* on the page is rasterised, so the text underneath is really gone. | | **Form fields** | Reads the AcroForm, fills it, and flattens the values into the page so they cannot be edited back. | | **Signature** | Draw it with a mouse or finger, or load a picture; the empty margin is trimmed and it is stamped where you choose. | | **Extract images** | Recovers the pictures stored inside the PDF at their original resolution. | | **Compress, three ways** | *Photos only* re-encodes the JPEGs and leaves the text as text; *lossless* runs qpdf over the result; *every page* rasterises, with an optional greyscale pass. | | **Batch** | *One file per source* — the same tools on every loaded document, one output each. | | **Share locked** | Wrap the finished PDF in a single HTML file that asks for a PIN — AES-256-GCM, the same container [LockHTML](https://github.com/drsamonline/lockhtml) writes, so either viewer opens either file. | | **Page labels** | The numbers a reader *sees*: i, ii, iii for the front matter and 1, 2, 3 for the body, written as a `/PageLabels` tree. | | **Compare** | Reads the text of the first two documents and reports the pages that differ, with the first line that changed. | | **A whole folder** | Pick a folder, and every PDF in it is processed and written to an `out` folder beside it. Chrome, Edge and Android Chrome only — the button says so when the browser cannot. | | **Insert blank pages** | Drop an empty page after the selection, sized like the page before it. | | **Interface languages** | English, हिन्दी and ગુજરાતી for the interface, switched in the header and remembered. | | **Remembered tools** | Your tool settings come back on the next visit; *Reset tools* forgets them. | | **Flatten & strip** | Flatten form fields, or remove the metadata before sending a file on. | | **Page numbers** | Four formats, four positions, starting number, size. | | **Metadata** | Title, author, subject, keywords. | | **Compress** | Renders each page to JPEG at a chosen DPI and quality, then rebuilds. | | **Images → PDF** | PNG and JPEG, one image per page. | | **Open a protected PDF** | Asks for the password, then lets you edit it — and keeps the protection on the way out unless you set a new one. | | **Password protect** | AES-256, with user/owner passwords and permissions for printing, copying, modifying. | | **Unlock** | Remove a password you already know, in the browser. | | **Extract text** | From a digital PDF → `.txt`. | | **OCR** | From a scan. The engine ships beside the app, so it works offline on the first try. | | **Credits** | All bundled libraries credited in-app and in `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md`. | | **Themes** | Dark, light, high-contrast. | | **Network counter** | Every `fetch` and `XMLHttpRequest` this page makes, listed in the app. A fresh copy reads `0 requests`. | | **Self-test** | Proves merging, rotating, cropping and AES-256 work — on your machine, in your tab. | | **Command palette** | `Ctrl-K` — every tool by name. | | **Undo / redo** | `Ctrl-Z` and `Shift-Ctrl-Z` across rotate, delete, duplicate, move and loading files. | | **Keyboard** | `Alt-←` / `Alt-→` moves the selected pages; the grid is a labelled listbox for screen readers. | | **Shortcuts** | `a` select all · `d` deselect · `[` `]` rotate · `Delete` remove · `t` theme · `Ctrl-K` commands · `Ctrl-Z` undo · `Alt-←/→` move pages · `?` help | ## Command line The same two engines, without the browser. `pdfkit` loads pdf.js and pdf-lib from `vendor/` — the exact bytes the page inlines — so a file merged in a shell and a file merged in the app are written by the same writer. ```sh node cli/pdfkit.mjs info report.pdf node cli/pdfkit.mjs merge a.pdf b.pdf -o merged.pdf node cli/pdfkit.mjs split merged.pdf --every 10 -o chunk node cli/pdfkit.mjs watermark merged.pdf --text CONFIDENTIAL --opacity .12 -o marked.pdf cat report.pdf | pdfkit info - --json | jq .pages ``` Twelve commands — `info text merge split rotate delete order watermark number meta labels impose` — plus `-` for stdin, `-o -` for stdout, `--json`, `--quiet` and `--locale`. Node 18+, no dependencies, no network. Rasterising (PNG export, compress-by-rendering, redaction rebuild, OCR) stays in the app, because those need a canvas. **[cli/README.md](cli/README.md)** — the commands, the pipes, and why CLDR is used through `Intl` instead of being vendored. Also the one thing worth knowing if you want to launch it from the [drsamonline/CLDR](https://github.com/drsamonline/CLDR) tray launcher. ## Not included, deliberately - **PDF/A conversion** and **Ghostscript-class compression.** These need AGPL-licensed components (Ghostscript, PyMuPDF, CoherentPDF). Using them would force this app to be AGPL, which is incompatible with the licence below. The one engine that is permissive enough — **qpdf**, which is Apache-2.0 — is included for the lossless pass. - **Editing page content.** The toolkit rearranges and annotates pages; it does not edit text inside them. ## Downloads The same HTML in a shell, built from the same commit as the page you are reading. | | | | |---|---|---| | **In the browser** | nothing to install | [open the app](https://drsamonline.github.io/offline-pdf-toolkit/play/) | | **Windows** | portable EXE, 9.0 MB, no installer | [offline-pdf-toolkit-portable.exe](https://github.com/drsamonline/offline-pdf-toolkit/releases/latest/download/offline-pdf-toolkit-portable.exe) | | **Android** | signed APK, 1.2 MB | [offline-pdf-toolkit.apk](https://github.com/drsamonline/offline-pdf-toolkit/releases/latest/download/offline-pdf-toolkit.apk) | | **Linux** | single binary, 21.4 MB | [offline-pdf-toolkit-linux](https://github.com/drsamonline/offline-pdf-toolkit/releases/latest/download/offline-pdf-toolkit-linux) | Every release carries the app icon alongside the artefacts (`icon-192.png`, `icon-512.png`), so the downloads identify themselves in a file manager instead of arriving as a grey box. - **Rolling build** — , rebuilt from `main` on every push; the `releases/latest/download/...` links above always point here. - **Versioned release** — records what changed and why, with the icons attached. ## Files ``` app.html the application shell (~160 KB; the engines live in lib/) index.html landing page (root deployment) docs/index.html landing page (Pages deployment) docs/play/index.html the application, as Pages serves it docs/assets/ badges, screenshots, icons, sample PDFs (all local): two text documents, a photograph page, and one written uncompressed so the lossless pass has something to prove docs/play/lib/ pdf.js, pdf-lib and the pdf.js worker, loaded on demand docs/play/ocr/ the OCR engine: wrapper, worker, two LSTM WASM cores, English data docs/play/qpdf/ the qpdf WASM runtime for the lossless compression pass pipeline/app_template.html the application source (readable) pipeline/landing.html the landing page source (readable) pipeline/app_extras.js the 1.3–1.6 tools (trim, impose, redaction, split, forms, signatures…) pipeline/app_i18n.js the हिन्दी and ગુજરાતી interface tables pipeline/app_extras_ui.html the panels for them pipeline/app_launcher.js the tool catalogue, the launcher and the all-tools sheet cli/pdfkit.mjs the command line over the same two engines cli/test/run.py the CLI suite: 44 checks, every file read back with PyMuPDF pipeline/kit_extras.html export / restore / undo / keyboard, kept in the source pipeline/build_pdf.py inlines the libraries + minifies → app.html pipeline/build_landing.py emits index.html + docs/index.html from landing.html vendor/ the three libraries, with SHA256SUMS checked at build time tools/badges.py draws docs/assets/badge-*.svg — no image service tools/shot.py takes the screenshots with headless Chromium (dev only) tools/make_samples.py generates the sample PDFs the demo and screenshots use tools/test/ the browser suites (126 checks) and run_all.py — run in CI on every push tools/fetch_ocr.py fetches the OCR engine once and verifies it against SHA256SUMS tools/fetch_qpdf.py the same for qpdf (Apache-2.0), the lossless compressor sw.js offline cache (identical copy in docs/sw.js) ``` `build_pdf.py` reads the three libraries from `vendor/`, verifies each against `vendor/SHA256SUMS`, writes them beside the app in `docs/play/lib/` and minifies the app's own CSS/JS/HTML on the way out. The readable template stays in `pipeline/`. `build_landing.py` emits both landing pages from the one source and stamps the build in the footer, so "am I on the new one?" is answerable from the page itself. The badges are generated, not fetched: an offline-first app should not need an image service to describe itself. `python3 tools/badges.py` redraws them, and every claim in them is checked against this repository. ## Licences - **App code** © Dr Sohil Momin — free for personal study, teaching and non-commercial practice; commercial use requires a licence; educational institutes free or at a discounted rate. - **pdf-lib** (Cantoo fork) — MIT · **pdf.js** — Apache-2.0 (Mozilla) · **tesseract.js** and **Tesseract OCR** — Apache-2.0 · **qpdf** — Apache-2.0 · **qpdf-run** — MIT. See [`THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md`](THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md). - **No third-party data is bundled** — no corpora, no fonts, no text of its own. Because the bundled libraries are permissive rather than copyleft, this app can carry normal commercial licensing terms. Two techniques here — re-encoding the JPEGs inside a PDF while leaving the text alone, and trimming a signature to its ink before placing it — were inspired by [PaperKnife](https://github.com/potatameister/PaperKnife). PaperKnife is AGPL-3.0, which this app cannot be, so **no code was taken**: the implementations here were written against the pdf-lib and pdf.js APIs already in the file. ## How to check it, rather than believe it - **Network panel** in the app: a live count and list of every request the page has made, split by whether it left this origin. Open a fresh copy, load a document, run OCR — it reads **`0 external`** throughout. The engine shows up as *this origin*, which is the point. - **Self-test** in the app: builds three pages from nothing, rotates one, crops one, encrypts with AES-256, proves the file will not open without the password, and reads the text back through pdf.js. Every line reports pass or fail, in your tab, on your machine. - **The build**: `vendor/SHA256SUMS` is checked before anything is inlined, so the shipped file is built from the exact library bytes on record. - **A Content-Security-Policy** in the built page: `connect-src 'self' blob: data:` — no other origin is named anywhere, so the browser itself refuses any other destination. The promise is structural rather than a paragraph. ## Handing a document to someone else A PDF with a password needs a viewer that asks for one, and most phones will just refuse to open it. *Share locked* writes something simpler: one `.html` file that opens in any browser, asks for a PIN, and then shows the PDF. AES-256-GCM with a PBKDF2-SHA256 key (250,000 rounds), a random 16-byte salt and a 12-byte IV per file, and the plaintext never leaves the tab. The container is the one [LockHTML](https://github.com/drsamonline/lockhtml) defines — same payload shape, same key derivation — so a file locked here opens in that viewer and the reverse. Only the PIN path is implemented here; LockHTML's shares, recipients and decoys are not. Two honest limits: a one-time view is enforced by `localStorage`, so it is one-time *on that browser*, not on the planet; and a six-character PIN is the floor, not a recommendation. ## Languages The interface speaks English, Hindi and Gujarati — the language button in the header cycles them and the choice is remembered. The Help text and the longer explanatory paragraphs stay in English on purpose: a mistranslated word in a document tool that handles clinical paperwork is worse than an English one, and those passages want a human read before they are translated. The 100 short interface strings were translated by a model and then **read by a native speaker** (Dr Sohil Momin, 2 November 2026) against a numbered review sheet — 100 pairs with the real screens in both languages — who reported no corrections needed. That review is the reason the interface can claim to be checked rather than merely translated. Labels added after 1.6.0 (the folder panel, Share locked, page labels, Compare, the redaction patterns) are **still English**: 47 of them, listed in the same review sheet. They need a second pass. `pipeline/app_i18n.js` is one file of plain string pairs, so a correction is a one-line change. ## Privacy Your documents are read into the browser's memory, processed on your own CPU, and written back to your disk. Nothing is uploaded, stored or logged, and closing the tab discards everything. There is no exception any more. OCR used to fetch its recognition engine from a CDN; the engine now ships beside the app in `docs/play/ocr/` (about 10 MB, fetched once by a human with `tools/fetch_ocr.py` and committed), so **the page makes no request to any other origin at all** — not for your document, not for the engine. The Content-Security-Policy says `connect-src 'self'`, which means the browser refuses anything else even if a future change tried. --- ## Built with Forge This repo is a **Forge** app and adopts the shared kits. - **Shared build workflow** — `.github/workflows/build-apps.yml` calls the reusable build in [`drsamonline/app-builder`](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-builder). On every push to `main` it builds a portable Windows **EXE** and a signed Android **APK** and attaches them to the `app-latest` release, so these URLs always track the newest build: - `https://github.com/drsamonline/offline-pdf-toolkit/releases/latest/download/offline-pdf-toolkit-portable.exe` - `https://github.com/drsamonline/offline-pdf-toolkit/releases/latest/download/offline-pdf-toolkit.apk` Built with [Forge](https://github.com/drsamonline/forge) by Dr Sohil Momin. ## Support Free, offline, accountless — and staying that way. If it earned its keep: | | | |---|---| | UPI (India) | `drsohilboi@ybl` — payee Dr. Sohil Momin, open amount, or scan [the QR](docs/assets/upi-qr.svg) | | GitHub Sponsors | [github.com/sponsors/drsamonline](https://github.com/sponsors/drsamonline) | | Ko-fi | [ko-fi.com/matneo](https://ko-fi.com/matneo) | | PayPal | [paypal.me/drsohilmomin](https://paypal.me/drsohilmomin?locale.x=en_GB&country.x=IN) | | My books | [Amazon author store](https://www.amazon.com/stores/author/B08ZT331LY/allbooks?ccs_id=aed72b9f-71d9-41dc-adee-e9368a317acc) | | More apps | [drsamonline.github.io](https://drsamonline.github.io/) | | Email | [sohilmomin2000@gmail.com](mailto:sohilmomin2000@gmail.com) | Nothing is gated behind it: no accounts, no tracking, no network requests.
open-materia-medica:
![Screenshot](docs/shot.png)

Open Materia Medica

344 remedy portraits, open to everyone.

A free, offline, open-to-everyone materia medica — the classical portraits in
plain language, each one set beside the real pharmacology and toxicology of the
substance it is made from.

Landing page  →   ·   Read the web edition  →  ·  Download for Windows (.exe)  ·  Download for Android (.apk)   ·   Download the Android app  →

> **Where things live.** The project **landing page** is served at > . The **web edition** > itself — the full 344-portrait library — is served at > , and its source > lives in [`docs/play/`](docs/play/). ---

Read it online  →   ·  

--- A plain-language **materia medica** as a self-contained, offline-capable static website and installable PWA — and an Android app that carries the whole library in your pocket. No build step, no server, no tracking, no accounts. > **Educational reference only — not medical advice.** Severe, sudden or > worsening symptoms need a qualified clinician. ## What makes it different Most materia medica flattens three very different kinds of statement into one confident voice. This one refuses to, and the separation is structural — it is built into the shape of every single chapter. | | | | |---|---|---| | **Classical claim** | what the old books say a remedy answers | tradition and testimony — **not** evidence that it works | | **Pharmacological fact** | what is established about the source *substance* | real science, but about the substance, not a preparation of it | | **Clinical evidence** | what trials of preparations themselves show | the hardest test, including the null results | A substance's pharmacology can be perfectly real while telling you nothing whatever about the remedy made from it. Keeping the three apart is the point. ## What's inside Every remedy page opens with a **source illustration** and the **essence**, then runs through the same blocks: **the traditional picture** (inner state → body → modalities → organ affinities) → **where the classical picture comes from** → **the substance in real medicine** → **look-alikes** → a **safety** note. | Path | What it is | |---|---| | `index.html` | Home / remedy index — all 344 portraits, one line each | | `search.html` | Offline full-text search across every portrait | | `diseases.html` | 66 conditions with their most-used remedies (jump-links) | | `repertory.html` | Mini-repertory: the most-used rubrics with first remedies | | `quick-reference.html` | The daily-practice fifty, plus every Boericke remedy in one line | | `compare.html` | Any two portraits side by side | | `study.html` | Study app — flashcards and self-test over the library | | `kingdoms.html` | The remedies by kingdom, with a distribution chart | | `families.html` | Sixteen natural families (snakes, spiders, the Kali family, …) | | `veterinary.html` | Animal conditions by species | | `agro.html` | Agro-homeopathy: crop, pest and storage problems | | `glossary.html` | 34 classical terms in plain words | | `evidence.html` | The research debate on ultra-dilute preparations, gathered neutrally | | `references.html` | Every source, cited once site-wide | | `basics.html` | Read this first — the beginner's primer | | `about.html` | The user guide — how to read a remedy page | | `compiled-by.html` | The compiler's page | | `license.html` | Licence and rights of use | | `remedies/*.html` | The 344 remedy portraits | ## Get the Android app The companion app bundles this entire site and runs it offline — no network, no server, works in aeroplane mode. **Install it** — download [`OpenMateriaMedica-1.0.apk`](https://github.com/drsamonline/open-materia-medica/releases/latest) (2.4 MB, Android 7.0+) and open it on the phone. Allow installation from unknown sources for the app you are opening it with. **Or build it** — the project lives in [`android/`](android/) and has **no dependencies**: no AndroidX, no Compose, no libraries. The only code is a single `WebView` activity. ```bash cd android ./sync-assets.sh # copies the site from the repo root into the app ./gradlew assembleDebug # or open the folder in Android Studio ``` `sync-assets.sh` exists because the site lives once, at the repository root — running it is what keeps the app and the website from drifting apart. ## Run it locally No build step. Serve the folder with anything: ```bash python3 -m http.server 8080 # then open http://localhost:8080 ``` Opening `index.html` straight from disk also works for browsing and search — the index loads as a script, not a `fetch`. Only the install prompt needs a server. ## Hosting It is a **static site** — drop the folder on any web host (GitHub Pages, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, a plain Apache/Nginx directory). **Live at** — served from this repository by GitHub Pages, straight from the default branch. What is committed is what is served. Served over `https`, it installs to a phone's home screen and works with no network at all: the service worker caches the entire library. ## Assets | File | Purpose | |---|---| | `assets/style.css` | The whole design system (one stylesheet) | | `assets/site.js` | Mobile nav, active-link highlight, back-to-top, reading bar, service worker | | `assets/search-index.js` | The offline search index, loaded as a JS global so search works from `file://` too | | `assets/icon.svg`, `assets/favicon.svg` | App icon and favicon | | `assets/icon-192.png`, `assets/icon-512.png` | Raster icons for the app manifest and launchers | | `assets/og.png` | Social preview card | | `sw.js`, `manifest.json` | Service worker and web-app manifest — the offline install | ## Editing - **Text and content** live directly in the HTML files. Remedy pages share one structure, so a find-and-replace across `remedies/` is safe. - **Navigation and footer** are a single canonical block repeated in every page. To add a page, copy the `
…
` and `
…

optical-kit: # optical-kit [![License: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-2e7d32)](LICENSE) [![test](https://github.com/drsamonline/optical-kit/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/drsamonline/optical-kit/actions/workflows/test.yml) **The shared optical-transfer core for drsamonline apps.** One file, no build step, no dependencies. This is the transport logic behind the transfer apps (`helioprism`, `blinkcode-ai`, `BLINKTRANSFER`), extracted once so it isn't re-implemented three times: - a **systematic LT fountain code** — the receiver needs *any* ~k frames, so a dropped frame costs time, never correctness (there is no back-channel to ask for a resend); - **self-describing frames** — session, sequence, block count, block size, total length, and a CRC, so a receiver can lock onto a stream mid-flight; - a **sender** and a **receiver** with progress; - a **pluggable codec** — the app supplies the QR or colour-matrix renderer. ## Why a fountain code A screen-to-camera (or speaker-to-mic) link has no way to ask for a retransmit, and a camera *will* drop frames. Numbered frames then need the receiver to catch every one — a coupon-collector problem. A fountain code needs only *enough* frames, in any order, so a loss costs a little time and nothing else. ## API ```js // send const sender = Optical.Sender(dataBytes, { blockSize: 1400 }); sender.session; sender.k; // tell the receiver these first const frame = sender.next(); // a Uint8Array; render it as a QR / matrix // receive const rx = Optical.Receiver(session, k, blockSize, totalLen); rx.add(frameBytes); // returns progress 0..1 rx.progress(); // 0..1 rx.result(); // Uint8Array, or null until complete ``` Lower-level pieces: `Optical.Fountain` (encode/symbol), `Optical.Decoder` (peeling), `Optical.Frame` (pack/unpack), `Optical.crc32`, `Optical.bytes` (text/base64). ## Verified `test-node.js` proves the round-trip, including dropped frames: ``` node test-node.js PASS 1024B block=1400 loss=0% k=1 overhead=1.00x PASS 51200B block=1400 loss=0% k=37 overhead=1.00x PASS 51200B block=1400 loss=10% k=37 overhead=1.11x PASS 51200B block=1400 loss=30% k=37 overhead=1.46x PASS 204800B block=2000 loss=10% k=103 overhead=1.20x PASS 524288B block=2000 loss=20% k=263 overhead=1.47x PASS 10240B block=800 loss=15% k=13 overhead=1.00x 7 passed, 0 failed ``` The browser demo (`demo/index.html`) runs the same round-trip in-page. ## Pluggable codec `optical-kit` moves bytes; it does not draw them. The app renders each frame with its own codec: - **QR** — e.g. `zxing-wasm` / `jsQR`, one frame per code; - **colour matrix** — a dense grid of colour cells; - **multi-code grid** — several codes per displayed frame. ## Support Free, offline, accountless — and staying that way. planner-pro:
Planner Pro

An offline-first planner that behaves like a tool, not a website.
Day, week, month and year planning in one quiet screen. Multi-profile, PIN-locked, no accounts, no servers.

--- ![Planner Pro — Today view](docs/screenshots/today-desktop.png) ## Why another planner Most planners are either a website with a calendar bolted on, or a subscription that owns your data. Planner Pro is a single small app you can open from a file, install as a PWA, or build into an APK/EXE. It loads instantly, works on a plane, and stores everything on your device. - **Zero runtime dependencies.** No React, no build step, no CDN, no fonts to fetch. ~210 KB of HTML/CSS/JS minified (290 KB readable). - **Genuinely offline.** A service worker precaches the whole shell; the app opens in under a second with the network off. - **Local-first data.** One versioned `localStorage` document, exported to JSON in one click. Your planner is a file you own. - **Fast by construction.** Views render in a single string pass with event delegation — no virtual DOM, no re-render churn, no spinners. ## Screenshots | Day | Week | |---|---| | ![Day view](docs/screenshots/day-desktop.png) | ![Week view](docs/screenshots/week-desktop.png) | | Year | Insights | |---|---| | ![Year view](docs/screenshots/year-desktop.png) | ![Insights](docs/screenshots/insights-desktop.png) | | Command palette | Mobile — Insights | |---|---| | ![Command palette](docs/screenshots/palette-desktop.png) | ![Mobile insights](docs/screenshots/insights-mobile.png) | | Mobile — Today | Mobile — Day | Light theme | |---|---|---| | ![Mobile today](docs/screenshots/today-mobile.png) | ![Mobile day](docs/screenshots/day-mobile.png) | ![Light theme](docs/screenshots/today-light.png) |

## Features **Planning** - **Today** — greeting, live clock, completion ring, streak, time-block count, open-task count, 7-day completion bars, brain dump. - **Day** — intention line, to-do list with priorities and inline editing, time blocks with a live "now" highlight, notes & reflection. - **Week** — real calendar weeks (not "every Monday forever"), weekly focus, weekly goals, seven day columns with completion counts. - **Year** — year theme, year goals, twelve month cards with goals and task progress. - **Archive** — finished years move out of the way automatically; restore, export or delete any of them. - **Carry over** — pull yesterday's unfinished tasks into today in one click. - **Repeating tasks** — daily, weekdays or chosen days; instances are created lazily when you open a day, so a missed day fills itself in. - **Day templates** — build a routine once ("clinic day"), save it, apply it to any date. - **Estimates and capacity** — put minutes on a task and see planned time against your day; the bar turns amber when you overbook. - **Insights** — a year heatmap, best streak, busiest weekday, 30-day trend and your most-used tags. Click any day to open it. - **Encrypted backups** — AES-256-GCM with a PBKDF2-derived key, unlocked by a passphrase you choose. Safe to keep in cloud storage; no recovery if you forget it. - **Bulk actions** — select several tasks to move them to another day or delete them (with undo). - **Markdown vault export** — one `.md` note per day and per week, zipped in the browser with a hand-rolled store-only writer (no dependency, verified against `unzip`). - **Focus timer** — start 25 minutes from the Schedule card; the countdown lives in the top bar with pause and stop. - **Subtasks** — one level of steps under any task, with a done count and an inline add box. - **CSV import** — `date,text,done,tags` pasted or chosen as a file; duplicates are skipped. - **Data health** — a check for missing ids, duplicates, dangling repeats and trash; repair fixes what can be fixed and never deletes a day or a note. - **Panic blur** — blur the planner when the window loses focus. - **In-place updates** — ticking a task patches the row and the counters instead of re-rendering the view: 1.7 ms instead of 66 ms on a 50-task day. - **Month view** — the whole month as a 7-column grid: tasks per day, done ones struck through, block dots, the month's focus above. - **Attachments** — drop a PDF or a photo on a day. Files are blobs in IndexedDB (8 MB cap), listed with name and size, opened or removed individually. Kept out of the JSON backup on purpose. - **IndexedDB storage** — the document lives in IndexedDB, gzip-compressed where `CompressionStream` exists, with localStorage as the fallback for `file://` and private windows. Existing localStorage documents migrate on first load. - **Month at a glance** — a mini calendar in the rail (and at the bottom of Today on phones) with a dot for every planned day. - **Share into the planner** — Chrome on Android can share text straight in; it opens quick add, prefilled. - **Swipe between days** — horizontal swipe on the day view on touch screens. - **Reviews** — a weekly review with an auto-generated summary (what got done, what didn't, what changes, next week's focus) and an end-of-day review that can seed tomorrow's first task. - **Tag filtering** — click a `#tag` anywhere, or type `#health` in search. - **Undo and a 30-day trash** — every delete is reversible, twice over. - **Drag to reorder** — order is meaning in a plan; move a task or block by its handle. **Craft** - Multi-profile with a 4-digit PIN, stored as a PBKDF2-SHA256 hash (120k iterations, per-profile salt) — never as the profile key. PIN asked on launch (configurable); profiles never see each other's data. - Command palette (`Ctrl/⌘ K`) that searches every task, note, block and goal, runs commands, and understands dates (`tomorrow`, `next friday`, `25 dec`). - Keyboard shortcuts for everything (`N`, `T`, `D`, `W`, `Y`, `A`, `/`, `1–5`). - Four themes — Midnight, Ocean, Light and System — with correct contrast in each. - Layout that actually fits: 3-column desktop, icon rail on tablets, bottom tab bar + FAB on phones, no horizontal scroll at 320 px. - 44 px touch targets, visible focus rings, `aria-current` navigation, reduced-motion support. - Print stylesheet — printing a day or a week gives you clean paper output. - Markdown export for a single day or the whole planner; **ICS export** for a day or a week, so the plan lands in your calendar. - Inline editing — click a task, fix it, press Enter. No dialog. - **Keyboard-first list** — `j`/`k` to move, `x` to tick, `e` to edit, `Alt+↑/↓` to reorder. - **Quick add reads English** — "call the clinic tomorrow 4pm #health" fills the date, time and tag, with a live preview of what will be saved. - **Copy a day** — pull yesterday's blocks and tasks into today (or any date) in one dialog. - A backup nudge if you have not exported in 14 days, and a prompt when a new version is cached. **Data** - One JSON document, versioned, with automatic migration from the v13 layout. - Debounced saves, a "Saved" indicator, corrupt-document quarantine, quota-failure warnings. - Import/export the whole database; export any archive separately. ## Quick start **Use it online** — [drsamonline.github.io/planner-pro](https://drsamonline.github.io/planner-pro/app/) **Install as an app** | Platform | How | |---|---| | Android / ChromeOS | Open the site → menu → **Install app** (or **Add to Home screen**) | | iPhone / iPad | Open in Safari → Share → **Add to Home Screen** | | Windows / macOS / Linux | Open the site → install icon in the address bar | | No browser install | Download `planner-pro.html` — one file, double-click it | ### Release downloads Built by CI from the tagged commit (Windows and macOS binaries are unsigned, so SmartScreen/Gatekeeper will ask you to confirm the first launch): | File | Platform | What it is | |---|---|---| | [`planner-pro.html`](https://github.com/drsamonline/planner-pro/releases/latest/download/planner-pro.html) | any | The entire app in one file — no server, no internet | | [`planner-pro-web.zip`](https://github.com/drsamonline/planner-pro/releases/latest/download/planner-pro-web.zip) | any | Offline web build: unzip, open `index.html` | | [`planner-pro-14.1.0-windows-setup.exe`](https://github.com/drsamonline/planner-pro/releases/latest/download/planner-pro-14.1.0-windows-setup.exe) | Windows | Installer (Electron) | | [`planner-pro-14.1.0-windows-portable.exe`](https://github.com/drsamonline/planner-pro/releases/latest/download/planner-pro-14.1.0-windows-portable.exe) | Windows | Portable, no install | | [`planner-pro-14.1.0-macos-arm64.dmg`](https://github.com/drsamonline/planner-pro/releases/latest/download/planner-pro-14.1.0-macos-arm64.dmg) | macOS (Apple silicon) | Disk image | | [`planner-pro_14.1.0_amd64.deb`](https://github.com/drsamonline/planner-pro/releases/latest/download/planner-pro_14.1.0_amd64.deb) | Debian / Ubuntu | Package | | [`planner-pro-14.1.0-android.apk`](https://github.com/drsamonline/planner-pro/releases/latest/download/planner-pro-14.1.0-android.apk) | Android | Debug APK — sideload it, or `adb install planner-pro-14.1.0-android.apk` | **Run from source** ```bash git clone https://github.com/drsamonline/planner-pro.git cd planner-pro python3 -m http.server 8080 --directory app # open http://localhost:8080 ``` > Opening `app/index.html` directly from disk works too — the app is written as > classic scripts, not ES modules, exactly so `file://` keeps working. The service > worker only registers over http(s), so "offline" is automatic either way. ## Keyboard shortcuts | Keys | Action | |---|---| | `Ctrl / ⌘ + K` | Command palette — search everything, run any command | | `J` / `K` | Move down / up the task list | | `X` / `E` | Tick / edit the focused task | | `Alt + ↑ / ↓` | Move the focused task up or down | | `N` | Quick add a task to any day | | `T` / `D` / `W` / `Y` / `A` / `I` | Today · Day · Week · Year · Archive · Insights | | `1` – `5` | Switch the main views | | `/` | Search | | `Esc` | Close palette, dialog or search | ## Data model ```js { v: 14, activeUser: "1234", users: { "1234": { name: "Sohil Momin", theme: "midnight", weekStart: 1, quickNotes: "", days: { "2026-11-10": { intention, notes, todos: [...], blocks: [...] } }, weeks: { "2026-11-09": { focus, todos: [...] } }, // keyed by the week's first day months: { "2026-11": { focus, goals: [...] } }, years: { "2026": { theme, goals: [...] } }, archives: { "2025": { days, weeks, months, years } } } } } ``` Days are keyed by the full date, so moving across a year boundary no longer writes to the wrong year (that was the v13 bug). Weeks are keyed by their start date, so a plan belongs to *one* week instead of repeating every week. ## Building ```bash npm install # dev tooling only: puppeteer-core + electron-builder npm test # 122 end-to-end checks in headless Chromium npm run build:single # one portable planner-pro.html npm run build:web # zip of the offline web build in dist/ ``` | Target | Command / workflow | Output | |---|---|---| | Web (offline, minified) | `npm run build:web` | `dist/planner-pro-web.zip` (−27 % assets) | | Single HTML file | `npm run build:single` | `dist/planner-pro.html` | | Android APK | [`.github/workflows/android.yml`](.github/workflows/android.yml) | `app-debug.apk` via Capacitor (JDK 21) | | Windows / macOS / Linux | [`.github/workflows/desktop.yml`](.github/workflows/desktop.yml) | `.exe`, `.dmg`, `.AppImage`, `.deb` via Electron | Desktop and Android binaries are built by CI, not on a developer machine: they need an Android SDK and per-OS toolchains. Push a `v*` tag (or run the workflow from the **Actions** tab) and the artifacts attach to the release. To sign them for distribution you will additionally need a keystore for Android and code-signing certificates for Windows/macOS — see [`build/android/README.md`](build/android/README.md). ## Roadmap The full, prioritised list of what could be added next — and what is deliberately left out to keep the app small — is in [ENHANCEMENTS.md](ENHANCEMENTS.md). Highlights: recurring tasks, ICS/calendar import-export, encrypted backups, optional cloud sync via a file the user owns, per-day attachments, a focus timer, and a "review" mode for weekly/monthly reflection. ## Privacy No analytics, no telemetry, and **no networking code at all** — grep the source for `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest` or `WebSocket`: there is none. The only way data leaves the device is a file you export. Nothing is sent after the shell is cached. The only outbound links are the ones in this README and the About screen. If you clear site data, the planner starts empty — export a backup first. ## Author **Dr. Sohil Momin** — built this to run his own days. [GitHub](https://github.com/drsamonline) · [Sponsor this work](https://github.com/sponsors/drsamonline) ## Sponsor Planner Pro is free for personal use and developed on unpaid time. If it earns a place in your day, you can [sponsor the work](https://github.com/sponsors/drsamonline) — sponsorship pays for the release builds and keeps the licence non-commercial. ## License [PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](LICENSE) — free for personal, academic, hobby, charitable and government use. **Commercial use requires a written licence** from the author. See [ATTRIBUTION.md](ATTRIBUTION.md) for the ideas and books this planner draws on.

profile-kit: # profile-kit **A small, reusable kit for a theme-aware, self-updating GitHub profile.** [![Landing page](https://img.shields.io/badge/landing%20page-open-2e7d32?style=flat-square)](https://drsamonline.github.io/profile-kit/) [![All projects](https://img.shields.io/badge/All%20projects-hub-2e7d32?style=flat-square)](https://drsamonline.github.io/) [![Offline-first](https://img.shields.io/badge/offline--first-yes-2e7d32?style=flat-square)](https://github.com/drsamonline/profile-kit) [![Built with Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/built%20with-Python-3572A5?style=flat-square)](https://github.com/drsamonline/profile-kit) [![Type: reusable kit](https://img.shields.io/badge/type-reusable%20kit-586069?style=flat-square)](https://drsamonline.github.io/profile-kit/) [![License: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-2e7d32?style=flat-square)](LICENSE) **Landing page:**  ·  **All projects:** Lift it into your own `username/username` profile repo — by hand, or by handing this repository to an AI agent — and you get a profile page that: - renders the right artwork and stats card for **light and dark** GitHub themes, - keeps its **badge counts and project list current** from the GitHub API, on a daily schedule, without you editing the README, - stays **self-contained and offline-first**: inline SVG, no external JS, no build step, no service to sign up for. Built and maintained by [Dr. Sohil Momin](https://github.com/drsamonline) — see **[All projects](https://drsamonline.github.io/)**. --- ## The three ideas it combines 1. **A theme-aware hero.** A hand-drawn SVG banner served through `` with `media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)"`, so GitHub shows the light artwork on a light theme and the dark artwork on a dark one — no JavaScript, just two committed files and the right markup. 2. **A metrics card, rendered twice.** [`lowlighter/metrics`](https://github.com/lowlighter/metrics) with the `classic` template, rendered once per theme into `assets/metrics-light.svg` and `assets/metrics-dark.svg`. Each render pins its own palette through the action's `extras_css` option, because metrics has no real light/dark switch (see the known limitation below). 3. **A self-updating README.** A small Python script regenerates the regions of the README that sit between HTML comment markers — a row of badge counts and a categorised project list — straight from the GitHub API, and a workflow commits the result daily. Everything outside the markers is left alone. Each idea stands on its own; you can take one, two, or all three. --- ## What's in the kit ``` README.md this file assets/hero-light.svg hero banner template (light) — edit the placeholders assets/hero-dark.svg hero banner template (dark) — edit the placeholders metrics.yml the metrics workflow — copy to .github/workflows/ profile-generator/ update_profile.py regenerates the marked README regions profile-data.json owner + markers + categories + curated repos update-profile.yml the workflow that runs it daily README.md how the generator works and how to configure it docs/ the kit's own landing page (GitHub Pages, served from /docs) ``` --- ## How to use it ### 1. Create your profile repo Create a public repo named exactly `username/username` (GitHub treats it as your profile README) and give it a `README.md`. ### 2. Add the hero Copy `assets/hero-light.svg` and `assets/hero-dark.svg` into your repo's `assets/` folder, then embed them in the README with a ``: ```html ``` **Editing the hero.** Both SVGs ship with three visible placeholders — `YOUR KICKER`, `YOUR NAME` and `YOUR TAGLINE` — plus the two-letter monogram `YN` in the corner circle. Open **both** files and replace those four strings in each, and update the `aria-label` / `` at the top of each file (they repeat the name and tagline for screen readers). Keep the two files byte-for-byte identical apart from their palette so the light and dark banners line up. ### 3. Add the metrics card Copy `metrics.yml` to `.github/workflows/metrics.yml`, replace `YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME` with your login, and run it once (Actions → *Metrics* → *Run workflow*). It commits the two SVGs to `assets/`. Embed them the same way as the hero: ```html <picture> <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="assets/metrics-dark.svg"> <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" srcset="assets/metrics-light.svg"> <img src="assets/metrics-light.svg" alt="GitHub metrics" width="480"> </picture> ``` Read the **Known limitation** below before you expect the languages panel to show anything. ### 4. Add the self-updating README regions - Copy `profile-generator/update_profile.py` to `.github/scripts/update_profile.py`. - Copy `profile-generator/profile-data.json` to `profile-data.json` at the repo root. - Copy `profile-generator/update-profile.yml` to `.github/workflows/update-profile.yml`. - Put the four markers in your README: ```markdown <!-- BADGES:START --> <!-- BADGES:END --> ... <!-- PROJECTS:START --> <!-- PROJECTS:END --> ``` - Edit `profile-data.json` — set `owner`, keep or change the `markers`, set your `categories`, and curate your repos. Run the workflow once to fill the regions. See [`profile-generator/README.md`](profile-generator/README.md) for the full configuration reference. ### 5. Turn on GitHub Pages (optional) The kit's own landing page lives in `docs/`. To publish something similar: **Settings → Pages → Build and deployment → Deploy from a branch → `main` / `/docs`**. The `docs/.nojekyll` file tells Pages to serve the files as-is. --- ## Known limitation: the languages panel is empty under `GITHUB_TOKEN` `lowlighter/metrics` works with the default `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`, but its **languages plugin renders empty** because the token is forbidden from reading a field the base query asks for: - metrics' base repositories query requests `stargazers { totalCount }`; - the repository-scoped `GITHUB_TOKEN` is **not permitted** to read that field, and the GraphQL call comes back `FORBIDDEN: Resource not accessible by integration`; - that leaves the repositories data unusable, so `plugin_languages` renders "0 Languages" with a bare, unstyled "Most used languages" link and no chart; - **the action still reports success.** There is no failing step and no red X, so the card simply looks broken with no error to explain why. **The fix:** a **classic personal access token with no scopes**, saved as the secret `METRICS_TOKEN`, is allowed to read `stargazers`. Create one (GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Tokens (classic) → Generate new token (classic); no scopes required for public data), save it as `METRICS_TOKEN`, switch the `token:` input in both render steps to `${{ secrets.METRICS_TOKEN }}`, and re-enable the `plugin_languages*` lines. The steps are spelled out at the foot of `metrics.yml`. **Also worth knowing:** `config_theme` is **not a real metrics option**. It is copied around the web often, but it silently does nothing. There is no built-in light/dark switch — light and dark have to be done with `extras_css` and **two renders**, which is exactly what `metrics.yml` does. --- ## Built with This profile is assembled from other people's work, and it deserves the credit. - **[lowlighter/metrics](https://github.com/lowlighter/metrics)** — the rendering engine behind the stats card. It uses the `classic` template with the `base` (header, activity) and `calendar` plugins, and its `extras_css` option to produce a matched light and dark pair from one configuration. Worth knowing: `config_theme` is not a real option and silently does nothing, despite how often it is copied around — light/dark has to be done with `extras_css` and two renders. - **[avgupta456/github-trends](https://github.com/avgupta456/github-trends)** — the idea of tracking lines of code by language over time, and the pattern of embedding a hosted SVG instead of generating one in the repo. # raylib-starter

[![test](https://github.com/drsamonline/raylib-starter/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/drsamonline/raylib-starter/actions/workflows/test.yml)
[![License: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-blue)](LICENSE)


![Screenshot](docs/shot.png)
**One C file, a fixed timestep, scenes, save and an ECS — on raylib.** The C answer to
`game-kit`: the same names, the same behaviour, and the same tests, on a 2.4 MB engine instead
of a browser.

Built for the 10 MB ceiling. A raylib game is one binary that runs on Windows, macOS, Linux,
the web (via Emscripten), Android and a Raspberry Pi.

## Use it

```bash
make              # the game        (needs raylib)
make test         # the suite       (needs only a C compiler)
make size         # fail if over 10 MB
make web          # the game in a browser (needs emsdk + raylib for wasm)
make wasm-core CC="zig cc"   # the core alone as wasm32, needs nothing installed
```

```c
gk_loop_init(&G.loop, 1.0 / 60.0);
gk_loop_tick(&G.loop, GetFrameTime(), loop_step, loop_draw, &G);   // fixed steps, then draw

gk_scenes_go(&G.scenes, "play", &G, NULL);                          // enter / exit / update / render
gk_save("progress.bin", &p, sizeof p);                              // magic + version + CRC32
gk_rng_seed(&G.rng, 12345);                                         // the same sequence as game-kit
```

## What is in it

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `gk_loop` | a fixed timestep: accumulator, a 0.25 s frame clamp, a 240-step cap, and an alpha for interpolation |
| `gk_scenes` | named scenes with `enter` / `exit` / `update` / `render`; an unknown name is refused rather than blanking the screen |
| `gk_input` | key down and pressed-this-frame, driven by the host — no engine types in the core |
| `gk_save` / `gk_load` | a struct on disk with a magic, a version and a CRC32, so a half-written save is caught, not loaded |
| `gk_ecs` | entities, component bags and systems over a bitmask; systems are handed the entity, so component access is O(1); `gk_ecs_queue_destroy` + `gk_ecs_flush` defer structural change out of a pass; fixed capacity, no allocation |
| `gk_rng` | mulberry32, **bit-identical to `game-kit`'s `rng()`** — verified in the tests |
| `gk_ease` / `gk_spring` / `gk_tween` | the eleven easing curves, the settle-time spring presets and a tween — **matching `motion-kit` to 1e-9** |
| `gk_camera` | world↔screen, follow with easing, zoom, deadzone, and bounds that keep the view inside the level |
| `gk_shake` | a camera kick as an elapsed-time effect: `make`/`start`/`step`/`running`, decaying to zero |
| `gk_machine` | named states, a transition table, enter/exit handlers; an event the table does not allow is refused, and names are copied into the machine. The demo's round uses one: warmup → live → finished |
| `gk_tween_chain` | several tweens stepped in order, with the overshoot carried so the chain keeps its total time |
| `gk_audio` | a thin wrapper over raylib's device: `init`/`load`/`play`/`stop`/`volume`/`playing`, volume clamped, calls routed and counted headless |
| `gk_tilemap` / `gk_move` | a grid of tiles with solid ids, and collide-and-slide: each axis swept and pushed back out, so a corner slides instead of sticking |
| `gk_atlas` / `gk_anim` / `gk_sprite_dst` | frame rectangles from a grid atlas, which frame is showing at time t, and where a world sprite lands on screen |
| `gk_tiles_visible` | the tiles a camera can see, as world rectangles, each with an optional atlas frame — a renderer walks the list, a test counts it |
| `gk_clampf`, `gk_lerp`, `gk_dist`, `gk_aabb`, `gk_circle_hit` | the maths `game-kit` exposes, same names |

### Targets

| target | needs | gives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `make` | raylib + a C compiler | `gk`, the desktop game |
| `make test` | a C compiler | four suites, 432 assertions, headless, no display |
| `make size` | raylib | builds, then fails above 10 MB |
| `make web` | emsdk + raylib built for wasm | `web/gk.html` + `.js` + `.wasm` |
| `make wasm-core` | only a wasm32-capable compiler (`CC="zig cc"`) | `web/gk-core.wasm`, and its size |
| `make snake` | raylib + a C compiler | `snake`, the second game |
| `make test-snake` | a C compiler | 35 assertions for the second game |
| `make link-check` | a C compiler | both games' real `main()`, 120 frames headless |
| `make bench` | a C compiler | the ECS benchmark, at a 4096 entity cap |
| `make cross CC="zig cc"` | a cross-capable compiler | the core compiled for five other machines |
| `make size-real` | an unpacked raylib in `RAYLIB_DIR` | the real binary, gated at 10 MB |
| `ndk-build` in `android/` | Android NDK + raylib for Android | the game on Android |

The core is engine-free: `main.c` compiles with `-DGK_NO_MAIN` and then contains no raylib at
all. That is what makes it testable, and it is why the stub exists.

## A second game, to prove it is a starter

`examples/snake.c` includes `main.c` for the core only and brings its own rules, scenes and
save. That is the real test of whether this is a starter or just one game: if a second game
cannot reuse the machinery, the machinery is wrong.

```
make snake          # needs raylib
make test-snake     # needs only a C compiler
```

Its suite covers turning (and refusing a reversal), movement on the ticker, eating, the three
ways to die (wall, self, and the legal move into the cell the tail is leaving), food never
landing on the snake, and the best score round-tripping through the save file.

## The demo game

`main.c` is also a small game, so nothing here is a sketch: three scenes (title, play, over), a
player and six drifting motes that are all entities in the ECS, collection by AABB, a 30-second
round with a two-second warmup phase the scene draws "ready" through, and a best score saved to disk. The world is 1280×800 inside a 640×400 window, so the
camera has something to do: it follows the player and stops at the level edges. A ring of solid
tiles closes the world, and the player moves through `gk_move`, so it collides with the border
instead of bouncing off it — the motes still bounce, through the ECS system. It exercises every part of the core, which is why the
tests can drive the real game headless.

## Verified

```
make test
326 passed, 0 failed    (the demo game)
43 passed, 0 failed     (harvest)
28 passed, 0 failed     (audio)
35 passed, 0 failed     (snake)
```

What the suite covers, all headless — no engine, no window, no display:

- **the loop**: 60 steps from 60 frames, a 1 s frame clamped to 15 steps, a 0.25 s frame × 4
  giving 60 steps, the step cap holding and resetting the accumulator, alpha in `[0,1)`
- **the RNG**: five values from seed 12345 compared against `game-kit`'s JavaScript output to
  1e-12, seed 1 likewise, `rng_int` inside its bounds and reaching both ends, `rng_pick` in range
- **the motion**: all eleven easing curves checked at t = 0.25/0.5/0.75 against `motion-kit`'s
  JavaScript to 1e-9, the `smooth`/`snappy`/`bouncy` presets against its stiffness and damping,
  and each spring's curve at seven points — so a C game and a JS game move identically
- **scenes**: enter before exit ordering, routing of update and render, an unknown scene refused
- **save**: round-trip, a size mismatch, a foreign magic, a future version, one corrupted payload
  byte caught by the CRC, and an empty payload
- **ECS**: create/get/has/remove/destroy, systems matching only the entities that hold the
  components they name, systems in the order added, a full world refusing more entities
- **the tilemap**: world-to-tile flooring (including negatives), solid ids and the out-of-bounds
  rule, free movement exact, a wall stopping the box flush on each of four sides, a corner
  resolving both axes, sliding along a wall without losing the free axis, a block mid-sweep
  stopping the mover there rather than at the far wall, many 1px steps landing in exactly the
  same place as one big sweep, a closed world, and a null or zero-tile map moving freely
- **sprites and animation**: atlas rectangles for the first, a row end, a wrapped row, the last
  frame, a frame past the end and a negative frame; a degenerate and a null atlas; animation at
  t = 0, mid-frame, the wrap, a non-looping anim holding its last frame, fps 0 as a still, a
  sub-range wrapping inside itself and a reversed range; sprite destination through a camera at
  zoom 1 and 2, and with no camera at all
- **visible tiles**: a view covering the map sees all 15, a 32×16 view sees exactly 3, a view
  outside the map sees none, the capacity is respected, a null camera means the whole map, a null
  map means none, and zooming out shows more
- **camera shake**: start/step/running, offset within the amplitude, decay towards the end, stops exactly at the duration and clears the offset, a finished shake is inert, a negative step does not rewind, zero duration never runs, restart resets, null-safe
- **the camera**: world↔screen round-trips at zoom 1 and 2, the camera's own point lands at the
  viewport centre, follow closes the gap and arrives, speed 1 snaps and speed 0 does not move,
  bounds stop at half a viewport, zoomed in the view may travel further, a world smaller than the
  viewport centres instead of clamping, unbounded leaves the camera alone, a zero zoom is repaired
- **the game itself**: start goes to play, seven entities spawn, the clock advances, the player
  stays in the world, walking into a mote scores, the round ends on the clock, the best is kept

### What was and was not verified here

Being precise, because "it builds" is easy to overclaim:

- **The suite was compiled and run** with `zig cc` (Zig 0.17.1's bundled clang), the only C
  compiler available in the environment this was written in. 320 assertions, all passing.
- **The raylib-facing half compiles**: `main.c` with `main()`, the three render functions and the
  key mapping compiles against `stub/raylib.h`, which mirrors raylib 5.x signatures. That catches
  a wrong call, not a wrong engine.
- **The real raylib link was not performed here.** raylib needs X11 and GL headers that this
  environment does not have, so `make` and `make size` are the two things to run on your machine.
  `make` itself is not installed here either; the commands those targets wrap were run directly.
- **Size, measured against real raylib**: **902,424 bytes** stripped, linked against raylib 6.2's
  own `libraylib.a`. That is 881 KB, 11.6× under the 10 MB ceiling. `make size-real` and CI both
  check it.
- **The core compiles for wasm32**: `make wasm-core` produced a **1,351-byte** module at `-Os`
  with only the loop reachable, which is the portability proof that does not depend on
  Emscripten being installed. CI builds it on every push and fails above **64 KB**, so a
  retained libc or a creeping dependency is caught rather than noticed later.
- **Three suites run in CI**: 320 assertions for the demo game, 35 for snake and 28 for audio, under gcc on
  Ubuntu, in the same workflow that builds the wasm core.
- **Both games actually run, past the title**: `make link-check` links the real `main()` of each
  game (not the `GK_NO_MAIN` core) against the stub and runs it for 120 frames while the stub
  presses start and the arrows on a schedule. The log reads `gk frames=120 draws=2533` and
  `snake frames=120 draws=712` — the loop, the scene machine, the key mapping, the tile renderer
  and the sprite renderer all execute. A run that never left the title draws 480, so the draw
  count is asserted as a floor: it is what proves the play scene ran.
- **Capacities are compile-time**: `-DGK_MAX_ENTITIES=8` was run through the whole suite to
  prove the core adapts, and the default is 256.
- **The Emscripten build was not run here** — emsdk is not installable in the environment this
  was written in. `make web` and `web/shell.html` are the pieces to run with emsdk present.
- **What still is not proven**: that raylib itself draws. Everything above runs against the stub,
  so a wrong `DrawText` argument or a bad window flag would only show up on a machine with a GPU
  and a display.

## The same motion as the JS kits

`motion-kit` and this starter now share a vocabulary, and the tests hold them together:

| From motion-kit | In C | Agreement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 11 cubic-bezier curves | `gk_ease_named("out")` etc. | 1e-9 at three points each |
| `smooth(300)` stiffness / damping | `gk_smooth(300)` | 947.203211111 / 61.553333333 |
| `snappy(250)` | `gk_snappy(250)` | 1148.803236 / 54.2304 |
| `bouncy(280)` | `gk_bouncy(280)` | 662.878584183 / 36.045 |
| spring value at time t | `gk_spring_at(s, ms)` | 1e-9 across seven samples |
| `tween(from, to, dur, ease)` | `gk_tween(...)` | endpoints, midpoint, clamp |

The demo game uses it: collecting a mote eases a ring outward on the `out` curve, which is the
same curve the JS kits use for the same gesture.

## Warning-free

Every configuration compiles with `-Wall -Wextra -Werror` — the real build, the headless core,
the stub link, both games, both suites, the benchmark, the five cross targets and the wasm
module. Seven configurations, no warnings.

That took two things: a `GK_API` attribute on the core's entry points, because a single
translation unit that does not use all of them would warn about the rest; and a
`GK_EXPORT` guard around the wasm-only `export_name` attribute, which the other five targets
would otherwise reject.

## The real binary, measured

`make size-real` links the game against raylib 6.2's own `libraylib.a` — not the stub — and gates
the result. Measured on raylib 6.2, linux amd64:

| | bytes | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `libraylib.a` | 2,847,000 | the engine, static |
| game + engine, unstripped | 1,091,856 | dead code already dropped by the linker |
| game + engine, **stripped** | **905,752** | 885 KB, with camera, tilemap and sprites |
| 10 MB ceiling | 10,485,760 | **11.6× headroom** |

`tools/x11_stubs.c` carries six weak X11 symbols so this links on a machine with no X server;
on a machine with X11 the real symbols win and the binary runs. CI does this link and the gate
on every push, downloading raylib 6.2 itself.

Plain `make` needs the X11 development headers on Linux (raylib's static library references
`XConvertSelection` and five others). Where they are missing, `make size-real` is the target
that still links, because it carries the weak stubs.

## Portability, measured

The core has no engine in it, so it cross-compiles anywhere a C compiler runs. `make cross` does
this on every push:

| Target | Core object | Verified |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `aarch64-linux-musl` | 4,024 B | ✅ |
| `arm-linux-musleabihf` | 2,964 B | ✅ |
| `riscv64-linux-musl` | 4,736 B | ✅ |
| `x86_64-windows-gnu` | 9,986 B | ✅ |
| `aarch64-macos` | 3,048 B | ✅ |
| `wasm32-wasi-musl` | 1,351 B | ✅ |
| `*-linux-android` | — | ❌ needs bionic headers, i.e. the NDK |

Android is scaffolded in `android/` (`ndk-build`, two `.mk` files, a manifest note) and is
honestly marked as unbuilt here. ARM is what Android devices run, so the instruction selection
and float behaviour are already exercised by the two ARM rows; what is untested is bionic and
raylib's Android glue.

## Why not archetype storage

The textbook ECS groups entities by their component set and stores component data inline, so a
system walks only matching entities and the data is contiguous. It is genuinely faster — and
`make bench` measures whether that matters here:

| entities | scan ns/entity | archetype ns/entity | ratio |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 256 | 8.1 | 0.46 | 17.7× |
| 1,024 | 17.2 | 0.47 | 36.6× |
| 4,096 | 8.9 | 2.18 | 4.1× |

The ratio is real and the absolute numbers are not: at the 256-entity default, one system run is
**2.1 µs** scanning against **0.12 µs** on archetypes — in a 16.6 ms frame at 60 fps that is
0.013% against 0.0007%. Archetype storage would cost component registration, inline storage and
archetype churn on every add and remove, to save a hundredth of a millisecond. It stays out, and
this table is here so the decision can be revisited if a game ever needs thousands of entities.

**The benchmark earned its keep anyway**: the first run showed 260 ns/entity, which turned out to
be a linear id lookup inside every component access — an O(n²) system. Systems now receive the
entity itself, `gk_ecs_comp(e, comp)` is O(1), and the same measurement dropped to 8.1 ns: a 30×
win on the shipped design.

## The stub

`stub/raylib.h` and `stub/raylib_stub.c` are the slice of raylib this starter uses: a virtual
clock, a scripted keyboard, and drawing that counts calls instead of drawing. Signatures match
raylib, so the same source compiles both ways, and adding a raylib call means adding it to the
stub too — the stub is the contract.

## Consumers

None yet — this is the first C kit in the fleet, written to be the starting point for the small
games. It is not wired into anything and changes no app.
